claim: The basolateral amygdala (BLA) is a key site where fear learning takes place through synaptic plasticity.
source: The basolateral amygdala (BLA) is a key site where fear learning takes place through synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific experimental data from this manuscript.

claim: Rodent research shows prominent low theta (~3–6 Hz), high theta (~6–12 Hz), and gamma (>30 Hz) rhythms in the BLA local field potential recordings.
source: Rodent research shows prominent low theta (~3–6 Hz), high theta (~6–12 Hz), and gamma (>30 Hz) rhythms in the BLA local field potential recordings.
evidence: This statement references existing rodent research findings about BLA rhythms.

claim: Several classes of interneurons (PV, SOM, and VIP) in the BLA can be critically involved in producing the rhythms.
source: Here, we create a biophysically detailed model of the BLA circuit to show that several classes of interneurons (PV, SOM, and VIP) in the BLA can be critically involved in producing the rhythms
evidence: This is a primary finding from the biophysical model created in this study.

claim: The rhythms produced by interneurons promote the formation of a dedicated fear circuit shaped through spike-timing-dependent plasticity.
source: these rhythms promote the formation of a dedicated fear circuit shaped through spike-timing-dependent plasticity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the computational model presented in the manuscript.

claim: Each class of interneurons is necessary for the plasticity.
source: Each class of interneurons is necessary for the plasticity.
evidence: This is a key finding demonstrated through model simulations where removal of any interneuron type prevents learning.

claim: The low theta rhythm is a biomarker of successful fear conditioning.
source: We find that the low theta rhythm is a biomarker of successful fear conditioning.
evidence: This finding is demonstrated through model simulations showing low theta increase only in learners.

claim: The model makes use of interneurons commonly found in the cortex and may apply to a wide variety of associative learning situations.
source: The model makes use of interneurons commonly found in the cortex and, hence, may apply to a wide variety of associative learning situations.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the generalizability of the model based on the ubiquity of these interneuron types.

claim: In the basolateral amygdala (BLA), the main site of fear learning in the mammalian brain, local field potential recordings (LFP) show prominent low theta (~3–6 Hz), high theta (~6–12 Hz), and gamma (>30 Hz) rhythms.
source: In the basolateral amygdala (BLA), the main site of fear learning in the mammalian brain (Fanselow and LeDoux, 1999; Tovote et al., 2015; Krabbe et al., 2018), local field potential recordings (LFP) show prominent low theta (~3–6 Hz), high theta (~6–12 Hz), and gamma (>30 Hz) rhythms (Seidenbecher et al., 2003; Courtin et al., 2014b; Stujenske et al., 2014; Davis et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: Recent rodent experimental studies suggest that BLA can intrinsically generate theta oscillations (3–12 Hz).
source: Recent rodent experimental studies (Antonoudiou et al., 2022; Bratsch-Prince et al., 2024) suggest that BLA can intrinsically generate theta oscillations (3–12 Hz).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent experimental work.

claim: Studies show increased low theta and gamma in LFP recordings after successful fear conditioning.
source: Furthermore, other studies show increased low theta (Davis et al., 2017) and gamma (Courtin et al., 2014b) in LFP recordings after successful fear conditioning
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Modulation of high theta is associated with fear extinction.
source: whereas modulation of high theta is associated with fear extinction (Davis et al., 2017), a paradigm that aims to suppress the association between CS and fear (Bouton, 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: VIP interneurons endowed with a D-current respond to depolarizing currents with long bursts, and to hyperpolarizing currents with no action potentials.
source: In our model, VIP interneurons endowed with a D-current respond to depolarizing currents with long bursts, and to hyperpolarizing currents with no action potentials, thus reproducing the electrophysiological properties of type I BLA VIP interneurons in Sosulina et al., 2010 (Figure 1A, top)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the model and shown in Figure 1A, reproducing experimental observations.

claim: VIP neurons exhibit short bursts of gamma activity (~38 Hz) at low theta frequencies (~2–6 Hz; peaking at ~3.5 Hz) in the baseline condition.
source: in the baseline condition, the condition without any external input from the fear conditioning paradigm (Figure 1B, top), our VIP neurons exhibit short bursts of gamma activity (~38 Hz) at low theta frequencies (~2–6 Hz; peaking at ~3.5 Hz; see Appendix 1—figure 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 1B and Appendix 1—figure 1A.

claim: SOM cells have a natural frequency of ~12 Hz in the baseline model.
source: In our baseline model, SOM cells have a natural frequency of ~12 Hz (Figure 1B, middle; Appendix 1—figure 1B)
evidence: This is demonstrated by model simulations shown in Figure 1B.

claim: PV interneurons are silent at baseline condition.
source: They are silent at baseline condition (Figure 1B, bottom)
evidence: This is shown in the model simulations in Figure 1B.

claim: When reciprocal connections are present between the PV interneuron and the excitatory projection neuron, these neurons form a PING rhythm.
source: However, when reciprocal connections are present between the PV interneuron and the excitatory projection neuron, these neurons form a PING rhythm (pyramidal-interneuron network gamma; Whittington et al., 2000), if the excitatory projection neuron receives enough excitation to fire (Figure 1C)
evidence: This is demonstrated in the model and shown in Figure 1C, with reference to the PING mechanism from literature.

claim: The frequency of PING depends sensitively on the external input to the excitatory projection neuron and the PV's decay time constant of inhibition (8.3 ms).
source: The frequency of PING depends sensitively on the external input to the excitatory projection neuron and the PV's decay time constant of inhibition (8.3 ms).
evidence: This is a finding from the model about the parameters that control PING frequency.

claim: Both the fear-encoding neuron (F) and the VIP interneuron are activated by the noxious stimulus US.
source: Both the fear-encoding neuron (F), an excitatory projection neuron, and the VIP interneuron are activated by the noxious stimulus US (Krabbe et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on experimental findings cited from Krabbe et al., 2019.

claim: VIP disinhibits F by inhibiting both SOM and PV.
source: As shown in Figure 2A (top, right), VIP disinhibits F by inhibiting both SOM and PV, as suggested in Krabbe et al., 2019.
evidence: This circuit mechanism is shown in Figure 2A and supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: VIP shows gamma bursts nested in the low theta rhythm before the onset of US.
source: before the onset of US, VIP shows gamma bursts nested in the low theta rhythm (blue trace)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A bottom panel.

claim: SOM fires at a natural frequency in the high theta range.
source: and SOM fires at a natural frequency in the high theta range (purple trace).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A bottom panel.

claim: PV is completely silent due to the lack of any external input before US onset.
source: PV is completely silent due to the lack of any external input (green trace).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A bottom panel.

claim: F is silent due to the inhibition from SOM despite its natural frequency of around 11 Hz.
source: (F) despite its natural frequency of around 11 Hz, is silent due to the inhibition from SOM (orange trace).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A bottom panel.

claim: After US onset, F shows a pronounced activity during the VIP active phase and outside when the SOM and PV inhibition fade.
source: After US onset, due to the longer VIP bursts and the US input, F shows a pronounced activity during the VIP active phase and outside when the SOM and PV inhibition fade.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A bottom panel.

claim: PV is active only when excited by F, and then gives inhibitory feedback to F.
source: PV is active only when excited by F, and then gives inhibitory feedback to F.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A bottom panel.

claim: VIP shows gamma bursting activity nested in the low theta frequency range with bursts duration affected by the presence or absence of US.
source: As in panel A, VIP shows gamma bursting activity nested in the low theta frequency range with bursts duration affected by the presence or absence of US.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B bottom panel.

claim: ECS and F are both active when both CS and US are present and VIP is active, producing a gamma nested into a low theta rhythm.
source: ECS (light blue trace) and F are both active when both CS and US are present and VIP is active, producing a gamma nested into a low theta rhythm.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B bottom panel.

claim: The evolution in time of the conductance (gAMPA) shows an overall potentiation over the second half of the dynamics when both ECS and F are active.
source: The evolution in time of the conductance (gAMPA) shows an overall potentiation over the second half of the dynamics when both ECS and F are active.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B bottom panel.

claim: ECS fires most of the time right before F, thus creating the correct pre-post timing conducive for potentiation of the ECS to F conductance.
source: ECS (blue trace) fires most of the time right before F, thus creating the correct pre-post timing conducive for potentiation of the ECS to F conductance.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Only the network endowed with all the interneurons leads to overall potentiation of the conductance from ECS to F.
source: We now show that, in the example used above, only the network endowed with all the interneurons and their associated rhythms leads to overall potentiation of the conductance from ECS to F in the timeframe used to induce the fear learning in experimental work.
evidence: This is a key finding from the model simulations.

claim: Experimental work finds successful learning after one or very few presentations of CS and US (lasting 1.5 or 2 s) interspersed with CS-only intervals lasting 30–40 s.
source: In general, experimental work finds successful learning after one or very few presentations of CS and US (lasting 1.5 or 2 s) interspersed with CS-only intervals lasting 30–40 s (e.g. see Davis et al., 2017; Krabbe et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on citations to experimental studies.

claim: The average ECS to F AMPA conductance robustly potentiates only in the network containing all three interneurons.
source: The average ECS to F AMPA conductance robustly potentiates only in the network containing all three interneurons (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A across 40 network realizations.

claim: All the full network realizations are 'learners'.
source: Furthermore, as shown in Figure 3B, all the full network realizations are 'learners'.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Learners are defined as those realizations whose AMPA conductance from ECS to F is higher than 0.12 mS/cm3 at the end of the 40 s interval.
source: We define learners as those realizations whose AMPA conductance from ECS to F is higher than 0.12 mS/cm3 at the end of the 40 s interval, which results in the systematic activation of the fear neuron F following most of the ECS spikes when only CS is presented.
evidence: This is a definition used in the model analysis.

claim: The PV cell is necessary to induce the correct pre-post timing between ECS and F needed for long-term potentiation of the ECS to F conductance.
source: The PV cell is necessary to induce the correct pre-post timing between ECS and F needed for long-term potentiation of the ECS to F conductance.
evidence: This is a mechanistic finding from the model about the role of PV cells.

claim: PV has reciprocal connections with F and provides lateral inhibition to ECS.
source: In our model, PV has reciprocal connections with F and provides lateral inhibition to ECS.
evidence: This describes the connectivity in the model.

claim: Since the lateral inhibition is weaker than the feedback inhibition, PV tends to bias ECS to fire before F.
source: Since the lateral inhibition is weaker than the feedback inhibition, PV tends to bias ECS to fire before F.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation from the model.

claim: The depression-dominated rule leads to depression rather than potentiation unless the PING is periodically interrupted.
source: However, although such a low excitation regime establishes the correct fine timing for potentiation, it is not sufficient to lead to potentiation (Figure 4A, Appendix 1—figure 2C): the depression-dominated rule leads to depression rather than potentiation unless the PING is periodically interrupted.
evidence: This is a key mechanistic finding from the model shown in Figure 4A and Appendix 1—figure 2C.

claim: During the pauses, made possible only in the full network by the presence of VIP and SOM, the history-dependent build-up of depression decays back to baseline, allowing potentiation to occur on the next ECS/F active phase.
source: During the pauses, made possible only in the full network by the presence of VIP and SOM, the history-dependent build-up of depression decays back to baseline, allowing potentiation to occur on the next ECS/F active phase.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation from the model about how pauses enable potentiation.

claim: The network with multiple heterogeneous neurons very robustly produces potentiation between the ECS and F affected by CS and US, respectively, during fear training.
source: We find that the network very robustly produces potentiation between the ECS and F affected by CS and US, respectively, during fear training.
evidence: This is a finding from the expanded model with multiple neurons of each type.

claim: Only the realizations of the full network learn the association between CS and fear.
source: This larger network corroborates the results obtained for the single neuron network: only the realizations of the full network learn the association between CS and fear (Figure 5D, left)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D left panel.

claim: All network realizations with all interneurons become learners in less than 40 seconds.
source: and all those network realizations become learners in less than 40 seconds (Figure 5D, right).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D right panel.

claim: There is a striking failure of plasticity if any interneuron type is removed from the network.
source: Similarly, there is a striking failure of plasticity if any interneuron type is removed from the network; even partial plasticity does not arise.
evidence: This is a key finding from the model simulations.

claim: Fear conditioning leads to an increase in low theta frequency power of the network spiking activity compared to the pre-conditioned level.
source: We find that fear conditioning leads to an increase in low theta frequency power of the network spiking activity compared to the pre-conditioned level (Figure 6A and B)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: There is no change in the high theta power after fear conditioning.
source: there is no change in the high theta power.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations.

claim: The LFP reveals a low theta power increase when considering the peak of the low theta power, and no significant variation in the high theta power.
source: We also find that the LFP, modeled as the linear sum of all the AMPA, GABA, NaP-, D-, and H- currents in the network, similarly reveals a low theta power increase when considering the peak of the low theta power, and no significant variation in the high theta power again when considering the peak of the high theta power (Figure 6C, D and E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C, D, and E.

claim: These results are consistent with the experimental findings in Davis et al., 2017.
source: These results are consistent with the experimental findings in Davis et al., 2017.
evidence: This compares model results to experimental findings.

claim: The newly potentiated AMPA synapse from ECS to F ensures F is active after fear conditioning, thus generating strong currents in the PV cells to which it has strong connections.
source: Specifically, the newly potentiated AMPA synapse from ECS to F ensures F is active after fear conditioning, thus generating strong currents in the PV cells to which it has strong connections (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation shown in Figure 6F.

claim: It is the AMPA currents to the PV interneurons that are directly responsible for the low theta increase.
source: It is the AMPA currents to the PV interneurons that are directly responsible for the low theta increase
evidence: This is a mechanistic finding from the model analysis.

claim: The low theta increase is due to added excitation provided by the new learned pathway.
source: Thus, the low theta increase is due to added excitation provided by the new learned pathway.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation from the model.

claim: The AMPA currents are the major contributor to the low theta increase.
source: We find that the AMPA currents are the major contributor to the low theta increase.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis.

claim: Both the AMPA and GABA currents contribute to the power increase in the low theta frequency range.
source: Although both the AMPA and GABA currents contribute to the power increase in the low theta frequency range (Figure 6G)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The AMPA currents show a dramatic power increase relative to the baseline (the average power ratio of AMPA and GABA post- vs pre-conditioning across 20 network realizations is 3*103 and 4.6, respectively).
source: the AMPA currents show a dramatic power increase relative to the baseline (the average power ratio of AMPA and GABA post- vs pre-conditioning across 20 network realizations is 3*103 and 4.6, respectively).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the model analysis.

claim: The low theta power increase is completely absent after fear conditioning in those network realizations that display no signs of learning.
source: Notably, the low theta power increase is completely absent after fear conditioning in those network realizations that display no signs of learning (Figure 6B, C, D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B, C, D comparing learners and non-learners.

claim: The low theta power change is a biomarker of successful fear conditioning: it occurs when there is learning and does not occur when there is no learning.
source: This suggests that the low theta power change is a biomarker of successful fear conditioning: it occurs when there is learning and does not occur when there is no learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model results comparing learners and non-learners.

claim: VIP interneurons, PV interneurons, and SOM interneurons in the BLA may be centrally involved in producing the experimentally measured rhythms based on the biophysical properties of these interneurons.
source: We show that VIP interneurons, PV interneurons, and SOM interneurons in the BLA may be centrally involved in producing the experimentally measured rhythms based on the biophysical properties of these interneurons.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the model.

claim: The gamma oscillation is associated with PV cell interaction with excitatory cells to produce PING.
source: the gamma oscillation is associated with PV cell interaction with excitatory cells to produce PING
evidence: This is a mechanistic finding from the model.

claim: VIP cells produce low theta due to their intrinsic D-current.
source: VIP cells produce low theta due to their intrinsic D-current
evidence: This is a mechanistic finding from the model.

claim: SOM cells help produce the high theta rhythm due to persistent sodium current (NaP-current) and H-currents.
source: SOM cells help produce the high theta rhythm due to persistent sodium current (NaP-current) and H-currents.
evidence: This is a mechanistic finding from the model.

claim: The rhythmic dynamics produced by VIP and PV cells both play a crucial role in the instantiation of plasticity during associative learning by promoting the formation of a dedicated fear circuit shaped through spike-timing-dependence.
source: Moreover, we show that the rhythmic dynamics produced by VIP and PV cells both play a crucial role in the instantiation of plasticity during associative learning by promoting the formation of a dedicated fear circuit shaped through spike-timing-dependence
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the model.

claim: The removal of any of the interneuron types from the circuit leads to failure of the plasticity needed for associative fear learning.
source: and the removal of any of the interneuron types from the circuit leads to failure of the plasticity needed for associative fear learning.
evidence: This is a key finding from the model simulations.

claim: The presence of SOM cells is crucial for plasticity in the model since they help to produce the necessary pauses in the excitatory projection cell activity.
source: We note that the presence of SOM cells is crucial for plasticity in our model since they help to produce the necessary pauses in the excitatory projection cell activity.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation from the model.

claim: The BLA SOM cells do not necessarily have to be the only source of the high theta observed in the BLA during fear learning.
source: The BLA SOM cells do not necessarily have to be the only source of the high theta observed in the BLA during fear learning
evidence: This is a caveat about the model's interpretation.

claim: The high theta detected in the LFP of the BLA also originates from the prefrontal cortex and/or the hippocampus.
source: the high theta detected in the LFP of the BLA also originates from the prefrontal cortex and/or the hippocampus (Stujenske et al., 2014; Stujenske et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on citations to experimental work.

claim: The model replicates the experimental increase in the low theta after successful training.
source: Finally, we replicate the experimental increase in the low theta after successful training (Davis et al., 2017)
evidence: This compares model results to experimental findings.

claim: The increase in low theta power does not appear in the absence of learning.
source: and determine that this is a biomarker of fear learning, that is the increase in low theta power does not appear in the absence of learning.
evidence: This is a finding from the model comparing learners and non-learners.

claim: All forms of STDP require that there be an overlap in the firing of the pre- and post-synaptic cells.
source: All forms of STDP require that there be an overlap in the firing of the pre- and post-synaptic cells.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle of STDP.

claim: With the depression-dominated rule used in this study, depression is overall stronger than potentiation, unless there is fine timing among pyramidal cells in the gamma and low theta cycles.
source: With the depression-dominated rule used in this study, depression is overall stronger than potentiation, unless there is fine timing among pyramidal cells in the gamma and low theta cycles.
evidence: This describes a key property of the plasticity rule used in the model.

claim: With this rule, each interneuron plays a role in setting up this fine timing in the gamma and low theta cycles needed for appropriate plasticity.
source: With this rule, each interneuron plays a role in setting up this fine timing in the gamma and low theta cycles needed for appropriate plasticity.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the role of interneurons in the model.

claim: PV interneurons are important in creating a gamma rhythm with F when the latter is activated by the US.
source: PV interneurons are important in creating a gamma rhythm with F when the latter is activated by the US.
evidence: This is a mechanistic finding from the model.

claim: This gamma rhythm plays a central role in the fine timing between ECS and F.
source: This gamma rhythm plays a central role in the fine timing between ECS and F.
evidence: This is a mechanistic finding from the model.

claim: The critical requirements for plasticity are a pause of VIP firing within each low theta cycle and fine timing of the ECS (pre) and F (post) neurons in the active phase of the cycle.
source: As mentioned in the Result section 'Mechanisms by which interneurons contribute to potentiation during depression-dominated plasticity', the critical requirements for plasticity are a pause of VIP firing within each low theta cycle and fine timing of the ECS (pre) and F (post) neurons in the active phase of the cycle.
evidence: This is a key mechanistic finding from the model.

claim: The pause in VIP cell firing allows for activation of SOM cells, which helps to inhibit the ECS and F cells.
source: The pause in VIP cell firing allows for activation of SOM cells, which helps to inhibit the ECS and F cells.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation from the model.

claim: Without the pause, the ECS and F cells continue to fire, and it is a consequence of the depression-dominated rule that this would lead to depression.
source: Without the pause, the ECS and F cells continue to fire. It is a consequence of the depression-dominated rule that this would lead to depression
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation from the model.

claim: With a Hebbian plasticity rule characterized by a lower amplitude for depression than for potentiation, potentiation would occur at most of the phases of gamma and thus fine timing would not be needed.
source: With a Hebbian plasticity rule characterized by a lower amplitude for depression than for potentiation, potentiation would occur at most of the phases of gamma and thus fine timing would not be needed (Appendix 1—figure 4).
evidence: This is shown in Appendix 1—figure 4.

claim: The depression-dominated rule allows for regulation of the plasticity by modulation of all the kinds of cells that are known to be involved in fear learning as well as providing reasons for the known involvement of rhythms.
source: The depression-dominated rule allows for regulation of the plasticity by modulation of all the kinds of cells that are known to be involved in fear learning as well as providing reasons for the known involvement of rhythms.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the advantages of the depression-dominated rule.

claim: With the classical Hebbian plasticity rule, learning can occur without the involvement of the VIP and SOM cells.
source: With the classical Hebbian plasticity rule, we suggest that learning can occur without the involvement of the VIP and SOM cells.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about an alternative plasticity rule.

claim: The depression-dominated rule is necessary for other aspects of fear learning and regulation, such as preventing overgeneralization.
source: Although fear learning can occur without the depression-dominated rule, we hypothesize that the latter is necessary for other aspects of fear learning and regulation. Generalization of learning can be pathological, and we hypothesize that the modulation created by the involvement of VIP and SOM interneurons is normally used to prevent such overgeneralization.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the functional role of the depression-dominated rule.

claim: VIP cells may be important in establishing the kind of depression-dominated rule used in this model for the synapse between ECS and F.
source: VIP cells may be important in establishing the kind of depression-dominated rule we are using in this model for the synapse between ECS and F.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the role of VIP cells.

claim: VIP cells are known to corelease the peptide VIP along with GABA.
source: VIP cells are known to corelease the peptide VIP along with GABA (Bayraktar et al., 1997).
evidence: This is based on a citation to experimental work.

claim: The amount of VIP release is related to the amount of high frequency firing, that is the duty cycle of the gamma burst in each low theta cycle.
source: The amount of the release is related to the amount of high frequency firing, that is the duty cycle of the gamma burst in each low theta cycle (Agoston et al., 1988; Agoston and Lisziewicz, 1989).
evidence: This is based on citations to experimental work.

claim: The peptide VIP can act on second messenger pathways to inhibit potentiation.
source: The peptide VIP can act on second messenger pathways to inhibit potentiation; the pathways are complex and not fully understood, but in hippocampus they involve GABA transmission, NMDA activation, and CaMKII (Caulino-Rocha et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on a citation to experimental work.

claim: The relevant VIP receptor VPAC1 is known to exist in the amygdala.
source: The relevant VIP receptor VPAC1 is known to exist in the amygdala (Joo et al., 2005; Boucher et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on citations to experimental work.

claim: By inhibiting potentiation, VIP may change a Hebbian plasticity rule to a depression-dominated rule.
source: Thus, by inhibiting potentiation, VIP may change a Hebbian plasticity rule to a depression-dominated rule.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about how VIP affects plasticity rules.

claim: Studies using fear conditioning as a model of associative learning reveal that learning and expression of fear are not limited to the amygdala but involve a distributed network including the amygdala, the medial prefrontal cortex, and the hippocampus.
source: Studies using fear conditioning as a model of associative learning reveal that learning and expression of fear are not limited to the amygdala but involve a distributed network including the amygdala, the medial prefrontal cortex, and the hippocampus (Seidenbecher et al., 2003; Bocchio and Capogna, 2014; Courtin et al., 2014a; Stujenske et al., 2014; Tovote et al., 2015; Karalis et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on citations to experimental studies.

claim: The medial prefrontal cortex and/or the hippocampus may provide the substrates for the continued firing of the BLA neurons after the 2 s US stimulation.
source: The medial prefrontal cortex and/or the hippocampus may provide the substrates for the continued firing of the BLA neurons after the 2 s US stimulation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the role of other brain structures.

claim: It has been reported that the prelimbic cortex (PL) modulates the BLA SOM cells during fear retrieval, and the latter cells are crucial to discriminate non-threatening cues when desynchronized by the PL inputs.
source: It has been reported that the prelimbic cortex (PL) modulates the BLA SOM cells during fear retrieval, and the latter cells are crucial to discriminate non-threatening cues when desynchronized by the PL inputs (Stujenske et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on a citation to experimental work.

claim: Brain structures such as the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus have been documented to play a crucial role in fear extinction.
source: Also, brain structures such as the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus have been documented to play a crucial role in fear extinction, the paradigm following fear conditioning aimed at decrementing the conditioned fearful response through repeated presentations of the CS alone.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Fear extinction suppresses the fear memory through the acquisition of a distinct memory, instead of through the erasure of the fear memory itself.
source: As reported by several studies, fear extinction suppresses the fear memory through the acquisition of a distinct memory, instead of through the erasure of the fear memory itself (Harris et al., 2000; Bouton, 2002; Trouche et al., 2013; Thompson et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on citations to experimental studies.

claim: Davis et al., 2017 found a high theta rhythm following fear extinction that was associated with the suppression of threat in rodents.
source: Davis et al., 2017 found a high theta rhythm following fear extinction that was associated with the suppression of threat in rodents.
evidence: This is based on a citation to experimental work.

claim: A recent experimental paper suggests that the BLA can intrinsically generate theta oscillations (3–12 Hz) detectable by LFP recordings when inhibition is totally removed due to gabazine application.
source: A recent experimental paper (Antonoudiou et al., 2022) suggests that the BLA can intrinsically generate theta oscillations (3–12 Hz) detectable by LFP recordings when inhibition is totally removed due to gabazine application.
evidence: This is based on a citation to experimental work.

claim: Antonoudiou et al., 2022 draw this conclusion in mice by removing the hippocampus, which can volume conduct to BLA, and noticing that other nearby brain structures did not display any oscillatory activity.
source: They draw this conclusion in mice by removing the hippocampus, which can volume conduct to BLA, and noticing that other nearby brain structures did not display any oscillatory activity.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach from the cited study.

claim: When inhibition is removed in the model, both AMPA and intrinsic currents contribute to the network dynamics and the LFP.
source: In our model, we note that when inhibition is removed, both AMPA and intrinsic currents contribute to the network dynamics and the LFP.
evidence: This is a finding from the model.

claim: Interneurons with their specific intrinsic currents (i.e. D-current in the VIP interneurons, and NaP- and H- currents in SOM interneurons) can affect the model LFP and support the generation of theta and gamma rhythms.
source: Thus, interneurons with their specific intrinsic currents (i.e. D-current in the VIP interneurons, and NaP- and H- currents in SOM interneurons) can indeed affect the model LFP and support the generation of theta and gamma rhythms (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Bratsch-Prince et al., 2024 shows that BLA is intrinsically capable of producing a low theta rhythm with ACh stimulation and without needing external glutamate input.
source: Another slice study, (Bratsch-Prince et al., 2024), shows that BLA is intrinsically capable of producing a low theta rhythm with ACh stimulation and without needing external glutamate input.
evidence: This is based on a citation to experimental work.

claim: ACh is produced in vivo by the basal forebrain in response to US.
source: ACh is produced in vivo by the basal forebrain in response to US (Rajebhosale et al., 2024).
evidence: This is based on a citation to experimental work.

claim: The model implicitly includes the effect of ACh in BLA by increasing the activity of the VIP cells, which then produce the low theta rhythm.
source: Although we did not explicitly include the BF and ACh modulation of BLA in our model, we implicitly include the effect of ACh in BLA by increasing the activity of the VIP cells, which then produce the low theta rhythm.
evidence: This describes how the model implicitly accounts for ACh effects.

claim: Low theta in the BLA is known to depend on the muscarinic activation of CCK interneurons, a group of interneurons that overlaps with the class of VIP neurons in the model.
source: Indeed, low theta in the BLA is known to depend on the muscarinic activation of CCK interneurons, a group of interneurons that overlaps with the class of VIP neurons in our model (Mascagni and McDonald, 2003; Krabbe et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on citations to experimental work.

claim: The olfactory bulb produces and transmits the respiratory-related low theta (4 Hz) oscillations to the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, where it organizes neural activity.
source: Specifically, it is known that the olfactory bulb produces and transmits the respiratory-related low theta (4 Hz) oscillations to the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, where it organizes neural activity (Bagur et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on a citation to experimental work.

claim: The respiratory-related low theta may be captured by BLA LFP because of volume conduction or through BLA extensive communications with the prefrontal cortex.
source: Thus, the respiratory-related low theta may be captured by BLA LFP because of volume conduction or through BLA extensive communications with the prefrontal cortex.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about how respiratory-related low theta appears in BLA.

claim: High theta oscillations are known to be produced by the hippocampus during various brain functions and behavioral states, including during spatial exploration and memory formation/retrieval.
source: Furthermore, high theta oscillations are known to be produced by the hippocampus during various brain functions and behavioral states, including during spatial exploration (Vanderwolf, 1969) and memory formation/retrieval (Raghavachari et al., 2001), which are both involved in fear conditioning.
evidence: This is based on citations to experimental work.

claim: The model predicts that blockade of D-current in VIP interneurons (or silencing VIP interneurons) will both diminish low theta and prevent fear learning.
source: Our model predicts that blockade of D-current in VIP interneurons (or silencing VIP interneurons) will both diminish low theta and prevent fear learning.
evidence: This is a testable prediction from the model.

claim: The model assumes the absence of significantly strong connections from the excitatory projection cells ECS to PV interneurons, unlike the ones from F to PV.
source: Finally, the model assumes the absence of significantly strong connections from the excitatory projection cells ECS to PV interneurons, unlike the ones from F to PV.
evidence: This is an assumption of the model.

claim: Including strong connections from ECS to PV would alter the PING rhythm created by the interactions between F and PV, which is crucial for fine timing between ECS and F needed for LTP.
source: Including those synapses would alter the PING rhythm created by the interactions between F and PV, which is crucial for fine timing between ECS and F needed for LTP.
evidence: This is a justification for a model assumption.

claim: The model prediction could be tested experimentally by selectively silencing each interneuron subtype in the BLA: if the associative learning is hampered by silencing any of the interneuron subtypes, this supports the study.
source: This prediction could be tested experimentally by selectively silencing each interneuron subtype in the BLA: if the associative learning is hampered by silencing any of the interneuron subtypes, this supports our study.
evidence: This is a testable prediction from the model.

claim: All the interneurons are necessary to establish fear learning only in the case of a depression-dominated rule.
source: We found that all the interneurons are necessary to establish fear learning only in the case of a depression-dominated rule.
evidence: This is a key finding from the model.

claim: The depression-dominated rule ensures that fine timing and pauses are always required for potentiation.
source: This rule ensures that fine timing and pauses are always required for potentiation
evidence: This is a property of the plasticity rule used in the model.

claim: Interneurons provide both fine timing and pauses to pyramidal cells, making them crucial components of the fear circuit.
source: interneurons provide both fine timing and pauses to pyramidal cells, making them crucial components of the fear circuit.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the role of interneurons in the model.

claim: Evidence suggests that ECS activity should increase during the US due to the release of acetylcholine (ACh) from neurons in the basal forebrain (BF).
source: However, evidence suggests that ECS activity should increase during the US due to the release of acetylcholine (ACh) from neurons in the basal forebrain (BF) (Rajebhosale et al., 2024).
evidence: This is based on a citation to experimental work.

claim: Pyramidal cells of the BLA robustly express M1 muscarinic ACh receptors.
source: Pyramidal cells of the BLA robustly express M1 muscarinic ACh receptors (McDonald and Mott, 2021).
evidence: This is based on a citation to experimental work.

claim: ACh from BF should elicit a depolarization in pyramidal cells.
source: Thus, ACh from BF should elicit a depolarization in pyramidal cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of ACh receptors.

claim: The pairing of ACh with even low levels of spiking of BLA neurons results in a membrane depolarization that can last 7–10 s.
source: Indeed, the pairing of ACh with even low levels of spiking of BLA neurons results in a membrane depolarization that can last 7–10 s (Unal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on a citation to experimental work.

claim: Activation of US leads to increased dopamine release in the BLA.
source: Activation of US leads to increased dopamine release in the BLA (Harmer and Phillips, 1999; Suzuki et al., 2002).
evidence: This is based on citations to experimental work.

claim: D1 receptors are known to increase the membrane excitability of BLA projection neurons by lowering their spiking threshold.
source: D1 receptors are known to increase the membrane excitability of BLA projection neurons by lowering their spiking threshold (Kröner et al., 2005).
evidence: This is based on a citation to experimental work.

claim: Neuromodulator release should induce higher spiking rates and more sustained activity in the ECS and F neurons during and after the presentation of US, thus ensuring a concomitant activation of ECS and fear (F) neurons necessary for STDP to take place.
source: Thus, neuromodulator release should induce higher spiking rates and more sustained activity in the ECS and F neurons during and after the presentation of US, thus ensuring a concomitant activation of ECS and fear (F) neurons necessary for STDP to take place.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about how neuromodulators enable STDP.

claim: The effect of dopamine can last up to 20 minutes.
source: The effect of dopamine can last up to 20 minutes (Kröner et al., 2005).
evidence: This is based on a citation to experimental work.

claim: A solution to the problem apparently posed by the non-overlap US and CS in some paradigms of auditory fear conditioning may be solved by considering the roles of ACh and dopamine in the BLA.
source: Hence, we suggest that a solution to the problem apparently posed by the non-overlap US and CS in some paradigms of auditory fear conditioning (Krabbe et al., 2019) may be solved by considering the roles of ACh and dopamine in the BLA.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about how neuromodulators resolve a potential issue with the model.

claim: Even though ECS and F neurons have the ability to fire continuously when ACh and dopamine are involved, the participation of the interneurons enforces periodic silence needed for the depression-dominated STDP.
source: We note that, even though ECS and F neurons have the ability to fire continuously when ACh and dopamine are involved, the participation of the interneurons enforces periodic silence needed for the depression-dominated STDP.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation from the model.
